=== Overview ===
== John de Glasgu ==
On 2 February '''1259''', [[Space:John de Glasgu|John de Glasgu]] was recorded as chaplain of Bishop Gamelin of St Andrews.<ref>''Registrum Prioratus Sancti Andree'' (Bannatyne Club, Edinburgh, 1841), p. 173; [https://archive.org/details/libercartarump6900edinuoft Internet Archive]; [https://poms.ac.uk/record/person/3404/ People of Medieval Scotland, person 3404].</ref> The record does not call John “Master”, identify his parents or make him Gamelin's brother. Earlier ''de Glasgu'' bearers are documented from the late twelfth century, so John is not the first known appearance of the name.

'''Master John de Glasgu, '''  chaplain of Bishop Gamelin, at the time of the exchange, was a member of the household of '''Walter''', commonly called cardinal of Glasgow in 1258 bishop of St. Andrews in '''1258'''<ref>This was dated 1258, in the "Charter Book of the Priory of St. Andrew's", during the reign of King Alexander 111 of Scotland, 1249 - 1286  (RPSA., p. 173),</ref> and may be connected to '''1207''' - John, canon of Glasgow<ref>https://www.poms.ac.uk/record/source/1682/</ref>

==Kilbucho ==
==== Gamelin ====
'''Gamelin''' was parson of Kilbucho and a chaplain of Pope Innocent IV in 1254; he also served as Chancellor of Scotland from 1250-1263. (Watt, 1977, p.85). During the minority of Alexander III of Scotland and the political turmoil this situation engendered, Gamelin’s loyalties lay with the [[Comyn-46|Comyns]], his presumed grandmother’s family<ref>https://www.oxforddnb.com/view/10.1093/ref:odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-10325</ref>, Registrum, i, 127, seems to show him as parson of '''Kilbucho''' and to link him Gilbert (son of Richer) <ref>https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=BZkgAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA189&dq=Kelbechoc&hl=en&sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwib_PnksNnqAhWhVBUIHbOqBbkQ6AEwAHoECAUQAg#v=onepage&q=Kelbechoc&f=false</ref> so that Gamelins early connections may have been with the families of Adam, son of '''Gilbert''', and the '''Grahams''' as much as with the '''Comyns'''<ref> (see Watt, Dictionary, 209-10. 2 Buchanan, History of Scotland, 240)</ref> but in any case certain that he was a leading Comyn supporter.

== Kelso ==
=====William de Glasgu =====

'''Named as William Wau, or Wan, of the diocese of Glasgow elsewhere. Although 'Wau/Wan' doesn't appear to be a complete last name. Possibly - 'Household of Walter, cardinal of Glasgow' ? He held the benefice of Kilwinning - where the Glasgow Memorial stands today. 

There seems to have been an early rule against a cleric holding more than one benefice at the same time, but the dispensations from the operation of the restriction, recorded in the papal registers, are so numerous as to leave the impression that it was not much honoured in the observance. Luckily, applications for the granting of such dispensations have been the means of preserving information regarding a number of benefices which might not otherwise have been procurable, and in this way the name of an early holder of the chapel of St. Mary is divulged. In 1384 " Walter Wan, of the diocese of Glasgow," was authorised to hold a benefice in the gift of the abbot and convent of Kilwinning, "notwithstanding that he has the chapel of St. Mary in Glasgow." Three years later the same chaplain made a similar application with reference to a benefice in the gift of the abbots and convents of Paisley and Kilwinning; but likely enough these entries in the register refer to the one benefice, possession of which, if got at all, may not have been secured till 1387.

In 1395 "Walter Wan, priest," presumably of St. Mary's chapel, applied to the Pope to sanction his acquiring "the canonry and second prebend of Glasgow," value 14 marks, void by the resignation of Gilbert de Carrick, notwithstanding that John de Tonergayth has unlawfully held the said canonry and prebend for sixteen years and that Walter has a perpetual vicarage in the city of Glasgow. [Papal Reg. i. pp. 566-7, 584.] Here we have the earliest extant reference to the prebend of Glasgow Secundo, the chief endowment of which was the vicarage of the parish. Tonergayth, as a place, is heard of in 1327 when Eva, widow of Robert Avenel, gave to the bishop and church of Glasgow, for the weal of her soul and the souls of her predecessors and successors, and for the increase of divine worship in the church, the sum of forty shillings, yearly, payable furth of her fee of "Thunregeyth," [Reg. Episc. Nos. 278-9.] lands which seem to be identified with those now called Tundergarth, part of the parish of that name in Annandale. One "John de Tunnyrgayth" was clerk of the king's wardrobe between 1360 and 1362, [Exchequer Rolls, ii. pp. 19, 112.] but whether he or another of the same name was the interloping prebendary has not been ascertained.

* Roll composed by Walter Trayl, referendary:— Walter Wau, or Wan, of the diocese of Glasgow. For a benefice in the gift of the abbot and convent of Kilwinning, notwithstanding that he has the chapel of St. Mary in Glasgow.
Granted. Avignon, 13 Kal. Jan.

===== Matthew de Glasgu =====
'''This de Glasu is more firmly established as Matthew Glendonwyn but he grants 'his kinsmen, members of his household' William de Glasgu Kilwinning & Kelso and  Robert de Wilton, his kinsman, a benefice in the gift of the abbot and convent of Holyrood. '''

From a charter granted by Bishop Matthew Glendonwyn in 1408 it is gathered that either he or one of his predecessors had made a substantial alienation of baronial territory. By this writ the bishop, with consent of the cathedral chapter, gave to "his beloved vassal," William of Strivelyne, son and heir of the late Sir John of Strivelyne, knight, the lands of "Cadare," in the barony of Glasgow and shire of Lanark, to be held of the bishop and church of Glasgow, for payment of a feuduty of £4 yearly, and making suits at three head courts of the barony, with ward, relief and feudal services. [Hist. MSS. Corn. Report, x. Appx. i. p. 62. From the expressions "vassals" and "heir" it may be inferred that the charter was the renewal of a previous grant to one of William's ancestors. The witnesses are Symon of Mundavill, I.A., archdeacon; John of Hawik, M.A., precentor of the church of Glasgow; Sir Symon of Glendonwyne, knight; and Sir John of Hawik, priest and notary public.] The lands of Cadder were thus detached in classification from those which remained in the possession of the bishop's rentallers, but in relation to the severed territory the bishops were put in the position of feudal superiors. [ Diocesan Registers, i. p. 38. The editors, without citing their authority, speak of Cadder as a barony and, alluding to its being held of the bishop by ward service, comment on such a tenure being very rare in Scotland.] Parts of the Antonine wall stood on the feued lands<ref>https://www.british-history.ac.uk/no-series/petitions-to-pope/1342-1419/p566a
</ref>.<ref>
Volume LXIII: 7 Clement VII. Anti-Pope</ref>

Matthew de Glasgu. For a benefice in the gift of the abbot and convent of '''Kelso'''. Granted. Dated as above.

== Cavers, Roxburgh == 

=== 1679 ===

The Croune of London was carrying 257 prisoners of war that were being banished to the American Plantations. They were all '''Covenanters''' who had been captured at the Battle of Bothwell Bridge<ref>https://drmarkjardine.wordpress.com/2016/12/10/beyond-orkneys-fatal-shore-the-wreck-of-the-croune-10-december-1679-history-scotland/</ref>. 

The Covenanters were a 17th Century Scottish Presbyterian Christian sect. They were evangelical and militaristic, effectively governing Scotland for a time during the War of the Three Kingdoms. At nine to ten o’clock at night on Wednesday 10 December, '''1679''', The Croune was shipwrecked near the Mull of Deerness in Orkney. What made The Croune one of the most infamous shipwrecks in Scottish History was its cargo of human beings, their ill treatment and how they were abandoned to their fate, locked below the deck. Among the survivors were '''John Glasgow''' and '''William Glasgow''' of Cavers, Roxburghsire parish. 


Note: May be a connection to ''1655''', [[Glasgow-591|William Glasgow]] , who's great-great-great grandson has written a family history available here<ref>https://www.wikitree.com/photo.php/0/0a/Glasgow-590.pdf</ref>. Stating that the Glasgow surname was originaly '''Cameron''', devoted covenanters presbyterians - following Calvinistic theology and Gameronian principles.  The name 'Cameronian' was given to the most militant of the Presbyterian sects which sought to prevent any dilution of the Presbyterian faith

== Covenanters == 

The Covenanters were a 17th Century Scottish Presbyterian Christian sect. They were evangelical and militaristic, effectively governing Scotland for a time during the War of the Three Kingdoms. They also fought in the English Civil war, where they were defeated by the New Model Army of Oliver Cromwell.

The Covenanters did not recognise the Divine Right of monarchs to lead the Church, only Jesus. This caused them to fall foul of a succession of Kings – Charles I, Charles II, and James VII, who all tried to suppress their religious and rebellious activities.

<blockquote>1425, William Croyser, alleged priest, M.A detained Dunkeld disosce unlawfully, void by the death of John de Glasgu</blockquote>


=== William Glasgow: a conditional Polwarth–Cavers–Ulster family —16 October2026 ===

[[Glasgow-2462]] is the proposed, very uncertain working father of the traditional Ulster ancestor [[Glasgow-591]] and the Cavers Covenanter [[Glasgow-4138]]. This carries the existing possible identity with the Polwarth child [[Glasgow-1605]] into a concrete local family model. The Polwarth index names the child’s father as William Glasgow, and [[Glasgow-2462]] is already attached to that child with uncertainty. The three younger profile accounts are retained as possible stages of one life, not three proved brothers. Neither new father attachment is independent support for the other: both depend on the same child/adult identity and on the unproved identification of the named Polwarth father with the Inveresk man.

The Polwarth child was baptised on 4 April 1658. If baptised near birth, he would have been about 21 at the examination of the Cavers servant in June 1679, 26 at the Ormistoun servant list in 1684 and 31 in 1689. Those are compatible ages for the recorded adult and the later military tradition. The Ulster profile’s circa 1656 birth is explicitly a rough grandson-based estimate, not an age stated by a record; its guessed Glasgow-city origin cannot exclude a Borders childhood. The exact forename and surname, compatible sequence and existing Borders candidate make this a usable provisional life model. Polwarth and Cavers are distinct parishes in different counties, and the chronology supplies compatibility rather than an identifying age match. The Cavers setting is recorded residence/association, not a proved birthplace.

The Cavers man is the leading existing Scottish comparison for [[Glasgow-591]] because the records establish a Covenanter and wreck survivor before the reported 1689 episode, while a probable member of his actual parish survivor group, James Young, appears among survivors said to have reached Ulster. Waddell’s 1886 account says all fifty survivors reached northern Ireland; his revised 1902 account says only some and omits both Glasgows from its named list. The omission does not exclude William, but the revision and late publication weaken the blanket migration claim. The 1684 Ormistoun record also prevents assuming uninterrupted Ulster residence from 1679. The later family history’s 1689 service and settlement remain tradition, not verified military service. No particular crossing, return journey, unit or Irish residence is invented. Its Cameron-to-Glasgow surname-origin story cannot explain a man already called Glasgow in 1679.

The weakest stage is the proposed father’s identity. [[Glasgow-2462]] was born at Inveresk on 20 August 1639 and baptised the next day. He would have been only 18 at the 1658 Polwarth baptism and 16, nearly 17, at the associated Elizabeth baptism in August 1656. Young fatherhood is possible, but there is no marriage, residence or occupation connecting him with the named Polwarth father. An older, otherwise unidentified William is a substantial competing explanation. The named-child clause does not prove [[Glasgow-2462]]’s identity. The regional Polwarth/Gordon household of [[Glasgow-3107]] is a stronger local kinship lead than Inveresk alone, but supplies no father clause for William; no exact brother, uncle or father relationship with James is selected. This inherited father remains a very low-confidence default and would fall away on both new adult accounts if the child/father identification fails. No mother is selected for either adult, and no wife or mother is transferred from the Inveresk ancestry.

The Polwarth child could be a different man from the Cavers Covenanter, and the Covenanter could be different from the late family history’s William. The Hawick father [[Glasgow-2731]] in 1692 and Cavers groom [[Glasgow-3587]] in 1708/09 remain competing later identities for the Covenanter; neither is newly equated with him. The attached [[Glasgow-3370]] entry in 1694 does not independently establish the Polwarth man as her father. If later Scottish records identify the Covenanter continuously there, the family history’s permanent Irish settlement would need reconsideration. Other Scottish William candidates and the possibility that the late ancestor account is mistaken remain open. A missing contemporary Irish bridge is not an exclusion, but the combined identification is especially uncertain. No surname or Y-DNA grouping supplies these missing generations.

Two very uncertain local father hypotheses are selected from existing research; no new original inspection, certain relationship, identity merge or live WikiTree save. Existing child/adult records, vital fields, attached relatives and their grades remain unchanged. Connectivity counts retained profile accounts, including possible duplicates, and describes the selected model rather than a proved pedigree.

Sources: [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XTBH-RJS Polwarth William, 4 April 1658, father William: FamilySearch baptism index XTBH-RJS]; [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYL3-24Q Polwarth Elizabeth, 17 August 1656, father William: FamilySearch index XYL3-24Q]; [https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FOPR%2FBAP%2F4437421&tab=this Inveresk William, born 20 August and baptised 21 August 1639, Thomas/Agnes: reviewed Findmypast transcript OPR 689/1]; [https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=GBPR%2FCOVENANT%2F028558&tab=this Cavers William, examination June 1679, servant at Ormistoun: reviewed Findmypast transcript JC39/22]; [https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=GBPR%2FCOVENANT%2F028560&tab=this Ormistoun William, October 1684 servant list: reviewed Findmypast transcript PC8/8 and PC12/9A]; [https://archive.org/details/cloudofwitnesses00edin A Cloud of Witnesses, 1714, banished-prisoner list pp.274–276; early derivative source]; [https://www.wikitree.com/photo/pdf/Glasgow-590 William Melanchthon Glasgow, History of the Glasgow Family, pp.1–2 and 5; late descendant tradition]; [https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Annals_of_Augusta_County.djvu/21 Waddell, Annals of Augusta County, 1886 p.5 note 1; late blanket Ulster claim]; [https://archive.org/stream/annalsofaugustac00wadd/annalsofaugustac00wadd_djvu.txt Waddell, revised Annals, 1902 p.8; some survivors, neither Glasgow named]; [https://ulster-scots.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/USCN-Covenanters-in-Ulster-Tabloid.pdf Holden and Thompson, The Covenanters in Ulster, pp.6–7; modern secondary associate/route evidence]. ==Stichill household and court records —22 October 2026==

[[Glasgow-1440|Patrick Glasgow]], husband of Helen Fairbarn, is now assessed as the 92% confident father of [[Glasgow-1238|James Glasgow]], the 1712 Stichill child and later husband of Elizabath Tait. The 1712 Stichill James, explicitly indexed as Patrick Glasow and Helen Fairbarn’s son, is confidently inferred to be the James who married Elizabath Tait in the same parish in January 1740. An age of about 28, continuity in this small local surname family and the later household’s son Patrick (1742) and daughter Helen (1750), repeating both proposed paternal grandparents’ names, form a combined identity argument. Naming is supporting evidence rather than a mandatory rule or independent proof of each step. The specific Patrick/Helen household is independently established by their 1707 marriage entries and 1708–1716 children. Newly inspected printed court minutes place Patrick at Stichill in 1712 and appoint him a burlaw man in 1715; these add local continuity, not a father clause. The unsupported Uphall field is not a competing contemporary record. No concrete rival Stichill James family has been identified in the held material; this is not an exhaustive population search.

Newly checked printed court records: 8 November 1712, Patrick Glasgow in Stitchill was fined one shilling sterling for reclaiming his impounded horse; 10 December 1715, he was appointed one of five burlaw men. The 13 November 1739 body names Peter Glasgow, fined with two other men over carrying teind peas; the edition’s index groups this under Patrick. Retain that last identification as a compatible continuation, not a certain death/survival boundary. The manuscript court book was not inspected. These records concern the local Stichill adult, not independent identification of the 1667 Gordon child.<ref>[https://ia800706.us.archive.org/9/items/recordsofbaronco00sticrich/recordsofbaronco00sticrich.pdf#page=211 George Gunn (ed.), Records of the Baron Court of Stichill 1655–1807 (1905), act 111, printed pp. 166–167/PDF 210–211]; [https://ia800706.us.archive.org/9/items/recordsofbaronco00sticrich/recordsofbaronco00sticrich.pdf#page=216 George Gunn (ed.), Records of the Baron Court of Stichill 1655–1807 (1905), act 117, printed p. 172/PDF 216]; [https://ia800706.us.archive.org/9/items/recordsofbaronco00sticrich/recordsofbaronco00sticrich.pdf#page=240 George Gunn (ed.), Records of the Baron Court of Stichill 1655–1807 (1905), act 158, printed pp. 196–197/PDF 240–241; index p. 241/PDF 285]. Printed pages visually checked 22 October 2026; court manuscript uninspected.</ref>

92% is a subjective confident inference for James’s father Patrick in the Stichill Patrick/Helen household, including the 1712-child/1740-husband identification. The underlying parish images and the FamilySearch 1742 page were not newly inspected; a security challenge blocked the latter. Patrick’s identification with the 1667 Gordon child, the 1765 Swinton couple, the Leitholm Robert hypothesis and all mothers retain their separate assessments. No birth, death, place, spouse, parent selection or identity merge changes. The new court pages establish recorded acts, not biological kinship. WikiTree’s father control was checked on 22 October 2026 and was already confident; no new live certainty mark is pending.

[https://glasgow.phenotype.dev/branches/early-scottish-records/#chapter-stichill-patrick-james-confidence Full family comparison and next questions]. This local connection does not prove a medieval Borders pedigree or the Gordon–Kilclone hypothesis.
